citeAs: Chen, Lin, Jinsong Li, Xiaoyi Dong, Pan Zhang, Yuhang Zang, Zehui Chen, Haodong Duan, Jiaqi Wang, Yu Qiao, Dahua Lin, and Feng Zhao. (2024). Are We on the Right Way for Evaluating Large Vision-Language Models? arXiv.
creator: Lin Chen, Jinsong Li, Xiaoyi Dong, Pan Zhang, Yuhang Zang, Zehui Chen, Haodong Duan, Jiaqi Wang, Yu Qiao, Dahua Lin, Feng Zhao (Shanghai AI Laboratory; University of Science and Technology of China; The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
description: MMStar is an elite vision-indispensable multi-modal benchmark comprising 1,500 samples meticulously selected by humans to evaluate large vision-language models. It covers 6 core capabilities and 18 detailed axes, with samples curated from existing benchmarks through automated filtering and expert manual review to ensure visual dependency, minimal data leakage, and balanced difficulty.
name: MMStar
rai:annotatorDemographics: Three experts conducted the manual review process.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper validates annotation quality by reporting that MMStar samples underwent manual review of each sample and that LLM performance on MMStar is almost indistinguishable from random choice, which the authors use as evidence of significant visual dependency and minimal data leakage from LLMs.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Samples were first coarsely filtered by eight LLM inspectors; then three experts manually reviewed candidate samples to ensure each sample’s answer was based on understanding visual content, that selected samples covered a comprehensive range of capability assessment dimensions, and that most samples required advanced multimodal abilities. Difficulty was estimated using hit counts of 16 LVLMs and split into easy (12-16), moderate (8-11), hard (4-7), and tough (0-3), after which 1,500 high-quality samples were manually curated.
rai:dataBiases: The benchmark is explicitly designed to reduce two identified biases in existing LVLM evaluation datasets: samples that can be answered without visual content and unintentional data leakage from LLM/LVLM training data. The curation criteria require visual dependency and minimal data leakage, and samples answerable by more than 2 of 8 LLM inspectors are excluded.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by collecting samples from six existing multimodal benchmarks, then applying an automated coarse filter with eight LLM inspectors followed by expert manual review. The source pool was reduced from 22,401 samples to 11,607 after coarse filtering, and finally 1,500 samples were selected.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw source data consisted of samples drawn from six existing multimodal benchmarks: MMBench, SEED, MMMU, ScienceQA, AI2D, and MathVista.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: Even the best evaluated model scores under 60 on average on MMStar. The authors state they plan to expand MMStar into a larger, online test set and explore dynamic evaluation methods to maintain visual dependency and reduce accidental data leakage, indicating current scope is limited to a fixed 1,500-sample benchmark.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors applied an automated coarse filtering pipeline using eight LLM inspectors and retained only samples with hit counts of two or fewer. They also used hit counts from 16 LVLMs to split coarsely filtered samples into four difficulty categories: easy (12-16), moderate (8-11), hard (4-7), and tough (0-3), then manually selected a balanced final set of 1,500 samples.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that inappropriate questions and data leakage can lead to misjudgments of actual multimodal performance gains and potentially misguide LVLM research. MMStar is presented as a way to improve transparency, fairness, and reliability in evaluating multimodal models.
rai:dataUseCases: MMStar is intended to evaluate the actual multimodal capacities of large vision-language models, benchmark 6 core capabilities and 18 detailed axes, and support fairer assessment of multi-modal gain and leakage.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Eight LLMs were used as automated inspectors for visual dependency and LLM leakage, including GPT4-Turbo, GeminiPro, LLaMA-70B, Qwen-1.5-72B, and Mixtral-8x7B. The authors also used 16 LVLMs to gauge difficulty of candidate samples.
